newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurd faction begins fleeing last Iraqi stronghold.
newsitem.headline: Kurd faction begins fleeing last Iraqi stronghold.

text.p: The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) began fleeing its last Iraqi stronghold of Sulaimaniya for fear of an assault by its Baghdad-backed rival, a U.N. official said on Monday.

PUK administrators poured out as forces of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) overran three more key points, one a hill where only the day before the PUK said its commander Jalal Talabani had visited the battlefront.

"The PUK has simply left its offices. The theory is they are on their way to the Iranian border. I think it's a matter of hours before something happens," Mogens Hansen, U.N. security officer for the region, told Reuters.

"They're running because they're frightened," KDP Captain Sami Jabbar said of the PUK fighters while he and his men advanced in a convoy of cars, buses and pickup trucks mounted with heavy machineguns. Jabbar said they were 80-90 km (50-55 miles) northwes of Sulaimaniya.

Minutes later the KDP men came under fire. At least one militiaman was killed on each side during the clash near Kani Osman village. Brush fires, ignited by the heavy fire, raged in fields on either side of the road.

KDP militiamen said they could reach Sulaimaniya later in the day. But KDP politburo member Faisal Mirani said no decision had been made and for now they would head north to strategic Dukan dam to control its hydroelectric power plant.

In a statement the PUK said Sulaimaniya, 50 km (30 miles) from the Iranian border, was in danger of collapse and appealed to Washington to help it against the KDP, now aligned with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

"The U.S. administration speaks of southern Iraq, but Saddam's tanks, army and secret police are on the move in the north -- towards Sulaimaniya, which is in imminent danger of collapse," the PUK said in a statement from Ankara.
From the heights of Heibet Sultan mountain, however, there was no sign any Iraqi troops or armour were involved in the latest fighting, an assessment shared by Hansen, the United Nations commander.
Baghdad, which actively backed the KDP assault on the main Kurdish city of Arbil nine days ago, has denied taking part in further operations.

KDP morale was high, buttressed by anti-personnel carriers, artillery and other heavy weaponry seized from the PUK at Arbil on August 31. Busloads of fighters, some sporting the yellow headband of the KDP, moved into position.
"Come on, come on," boisterous KDP peshmerga guerrillas shouted to their comrades, offering free passage to Sulaimaniya. Civilian supporters waved KDP banners as the fighters passed.
The KDP's war booty included a Soviet-era T-62 tank, seven armoured pesonnel carriers, five Katyusha rocket launchers and truck-mounted heavy machineguns.
Inside the village of Degala and the city of Koi Sanjaq, both further to the west, there were no signs the PUK had made a determined stand when they fell on Sunday to the KDP.

The real skirmishes had taken place on earthworks near the main Sulaimaniya road, now littered with spent cartridges. Thousands fled for the Iranian border on Sunday in cars, trucks and even bulldozers.
Some took a grim view. In Kani Osman, 53-year-old Younes Abdul Aziz said: "I'm a poor man. I've nothing to do with politics. I'm concerned with making a living."
As Kurds headed for Iran, a senior KDP official who asked not to be identified voiced concern about a possible Iranian response on the side of the PUK.

"Of course we are worried. We don't want to press too hard. We would like to resolve this peacefully without fighting but there is a lot of momentum to keep going to Sulaimaniya," the KDP official said.
Most shops were open in Koi Sanjaq, a city of 80,000, on Monday as residents went about their business cautiously.

The KDP seized the international spotlight on August 31 when, aided by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, the militia captured Arbil. The United States retaliated against Saddam by firing 44 cruise missiles on southern Iraq.
